argentina.intro:
Argentina is a long country of big cities, wine valleys, high deserts, lakes and glaciers, and its food culture is built around shared meals, grilled meat and late dinners. Eating out is a central part of daily life.

This page explains what Argentina is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Argentina is known for tango, football, the Andes, Patagonia and Iguazú Falls. Its cities have a strong European feel, shaped by Italian and Spanish settlers, and its cafe culture is lively at any hour.

The country stretches from subtropical forest in the north to the cold tip of South America in the south, so the food and the scenery change a lot from region to region.

The asado, a slow grill of beef, sausages and offal over wood or coal, is the national meal and a social ritual. Empanadas, filled pastries baked or fried, are eaten everywhere, and every province has its own filling and fold. Milanesa, a breaded cutlet, and provoleta, grilled cheese, are common favorites.

Sweet things matter too: dulce de leche appears in alfajores, pancakes and ice cream. Mate, a bitter herbal drink shared from one gourd, is part of daily life. Malbec from Mendoza is the signature wine.

Buenos Aires is the usual start, with its neighborhoods, theaters and markets. Mendoza is the center of wine country, Salta and Jujuy offer colorful mountain landscapes in the north, and Iguazú Falls sits on the border with Brazil.

In Patagonia, Bariloche offers lakes and mountains, El Calafate has the Perito Moreno glacier, and Ushuaia is the gateway to the far south and to Antarctic cruises.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Argentina
sections.body:

Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. For a traditional meal, look for places that grill meat over wood, and check the photos for the cuts and sides.

If you do not eat meat, check the menu for vegetarian options, which are growing in the big cities.

Tipping around 10 percent is customary when service is not included. Many places close in the afternoon between lunch and dinner, so check hours. Book ahead for weekends in Buenos Aires and in popular tourist towns, and carry some cash for smaller places.

faqs.q: What is Argentina famous for in food?
faqs.a: Argentina is famous for asado, beef, empanadas, dulce de leche, mate and Malbec wine.

faqs.q: What time do people eat dinner in Argentina?
faqs.a: Dinner usually starts around 8 or 9 in the evening or later, especially in cities.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in Argentina?
faqs.a: Buenos Aires, Mendoza, Salta, Iguazú Falls, Bariloche, El Calafate and Ushuaia are popular.

faqs.q: Is Argentina good for vegetarians?
faqs.a: Meat is central, but big cities now have many vegetarian friendly places. Check menus on Restroze.

argentina/buenos-aires.intro:
Buenos Aires is the political and cultural center of Argentina and the most visited part of the country. This page covers the Buenos Aires region, with the capital city and its dining culture.

This page explains what Buenos Aires is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Buenos Aires is known for
sections.body:
Buenos Aires is known for tango, grand avenues, bookshops, football and a lively night life. Its neighborhoods each have a character, from the colorful streets of La Boca to the parks and cafes of Palermo and the old cafe culture of the center.

People here eat late and stay long at the table, and a meal can easily last two or three hours.

Steak houses known as parrillas serve the classic grill, with cuts such as bife de chorizo and ojo de bife. Empanadas, pizza in the local thick style, pasta and milanesa reflect the Italian influence. Provoleta and chorizo sandwiches called choripan are everyday favorites.

Coffee and medialunas, small sweet croissants, are the standard breakfast. Alfajores and ice cream with dulce de leche are popular desserts.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Buenos Aires
sections.body:
Plaza de Mayo, the Recoleta Cemetery, San Telmo market, La Boca and the Palermo parks are classic visits. Teatro Colon is a famous opera house, and many places offer tango shows and lessons.

If you have time, take a day trip to Tigre and its river delta, or cross the river to Colonia in Uruguay.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Buenos Aires
sections.body:
Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Parrillas, bodegones with classic home cooking, modern kitchens and cafes all appear in the city, so decide what kind of meal you want first and filter by area.

Popular places can fill up at night, so a booking helps.

The best months are spring and autumn, from September to November and March to May. Summer can be hot and humid. Tipping about 10 percent is normal, and a cover charge for bread and table service is sometimes added.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Buenos Aires?
faqs.a: Try a parrilla grill, empanadas, milanesa, provoleta, pasta, medialunas and alfajores.

faqs.q: What time do restaurants open in Buenos Aires?
faqs.a: Many open for dinner after 8 pm, and some stay open until midnight or later.

faqs.q: What are the best neighborhoods to eat in?
faqs.a: Palermo, San Telmo, Recoleta and Puerto Madero are popular. Compare listings on Restroze.

faqs.q: Should I book a table in Buenos Aires?
faqs.a: Yes for weekends and popular places.

faqs.q: What is a parrilla?
faqs.a: A parrilla is a grill restaurant that serves beef, sausages and other grilled meats.

argentina/buenos-aires/buenos-aires.intro:
Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, is a large city on the Rio de la Plata with a mix of grand architecture, parks, theaters and neighborhood restaurants. It is the best starting point for exploring Argentine food.

This page explains what Buenos Aires is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Buenos Aires is known for
sections.body:
The city is known for tango, literature, football and elegant cafes that have served coffee for generations. Its neighborhoods, called barrios, each have their own food and style, from the traditional cafes of Monserrat to the leafy streets of Palermo.

The food scene mixes Argentine, Italian, Spanish and newer international influences, and the city is also known for its natural wine bars and modern tasting menus.

Order a parrilla grill for a taste of the national classic, with cuts of beef and sausage. Empanadas, pizza with cheese on thick crust, fugazzeta and pasta come from the Italian side. Milanesa napolitana, topped with ham, tomato and cheese, is a favorite.

For breakfast, have a cafe con leche and medialunas. For dessert, try flan with dulce de leche, alfajores and helado.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Buenos Aires
sections.body:
Plaza de Mayo and the Casa Rosada, the Recoleta Cemetery, the San Telmo Sunday market, the colorful Caminito in La Boca, and the Palermo parks and gardens are the main sights. The Teatro Colon and the El Ateneo bookstore are loved by visitors.

If you want to see tango, many venues offer dinner shows, and some neighborhood halls hold open dancing nights called milongas.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Buenos Aires
sections.body:
Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Decide on the area first. Palermo has the widest choice, San Telmo has older places, and Puerto Madero has waterfront dining. Look at menus in the photos for cuts of meat and for vegetarian options.

For popular places, book ahead and arrive close to your reservation, since tables are often held for a short time.

Dinner often starts after 9 pm, so plan a snack in the afternoon if you get hungry. Tipping about 10 percent is customary. Taxis and rideshares are easy, and the subway is cheap but closes late at night.

faqs.q: What is Buenos Aires famous for in food?
faqs.a: Buenos Aires is famous for parrillas, empanadas, pizza, pasta, medialunas and dulce de leche desserts.

faqs.q: Where should I eat in Buenos Aires?
faqs.a: Palermo, San Telmo, Recoleta and Puerto Madero are popular areas. Compare listings on Restroze.

faqs.q: Is Buenos Aires good for vegetarians?
faqs.a: Yes, there are more vegetarian and vegan places each year, especially in Palermo.

faqs.q: Can I see tango while eating dinner?
faqs.a: Yes, many venues combine dinner with a tango show.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Buenos Aires?
faqs.a: Spring and autumn are the most pleasant.

argentina/cordoba-province.intro:
Córdoba Province sits in the center of Argentina, with hills, rivers and colonial towns. It is a favorite holiday area for Argentines and a good base for slow travel.

This page explains what Córdoba Province is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Córdoba Province is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for the Sierras de Córdoba, a range of low mountains with lakes, rivers and small towns where families spend the summer. The city of Córdoba has one of the oldest universities in the Americas, and the Jesuit estancias of the region are recognized for their historic value.

Folk music, craft markets and small guesthouses add to the relaxed feel.

The region is known for its sausages, cured meats and cheeses, and for the cooking of the sierras, which includes goat, trout and stews. Locro, a thick corn and bean stew, is common in cooler months, and empanadas are served in many forms.

Sweets include alfajores, regional chocolates and fruit preserves. The fernet and cola mix is the local drink of choice for many, and craft beer is popular in the mountain towns.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Córdoba Province
sections.body:
The Jesuit Block and the Sierras of Cordoba are on many routes. Villa General Belgrano has Alpine and German style food and a beer festival, while Alta Gracia is known for its Jesuit estancia and its link to the revolutionary Che Guevara. La Cumbrecita is a pedestrian mountain village.

The Camino de las Altas Cumbres offers scenic driving, and Mina Clavero is known for its river beaches.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Córdoba Province
sections.body:
Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. In mountain towns, look for places with outdoor seating and regional dishes. In the city of Cordoba, compare listings by neighborhood, since the center is busy and the student areas have many casual places.

Book ahead in January and February, when domestic holiday travel is heavy.
Summer is warm and busy, and winter is cool in the mountains. A car makes touring easier. Restaurants close for a break in the afternoon in small towns, so plan your lunch time.

faqs.q: What is Córdoba Province known for?
faqs.a: It is known for its hills, lakes, Jesuit heritage, hearty regional food and student culture.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Córdoba Province?
faqs.a: Try locro, empanadas, regional cheeses and cured meats, goat or trout in the sierras and alfajores.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: Cordoba city, Alta Gracia, Villa General Belgrano and La Cumbrecita are popular.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Spring and autumn are pleasant. Summer is the busiest.

faqs.q: Do I need a car?
faqs.a: A car helps if you want to reach the mountain towns.

argentina/cordoba-province/cordoba.intro:
Córdoba is the second largest city of Argentina and a center of education and culture. Its colonial buildings stand beside modern cafes and busy street life.

This page explains what Córdoba is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Cordoba is known as La Docta, the learned city, because of its historic university. The Jesuit Block, with churches and university buildings, is a World Heritage site, and the old center is walkable.

Students give the city a young energy, with live music, bars and street food in neighborhoods such as Nueva Cordoba and Guemes.

Local favorites include the lomito sandwich, a steak sandwich with ham, egg and cheese, and the chivito of the region. Empanadas, locro and grilled meats are common. Alfajores cordobeses, sweets with dulce de leche and coconut, are a local gift.

The fernet with cola mix is the favorite drink of the city. Cafes serve medialunas and strong coffee through the day.

The Jesuit Block, the Cathedral, the Cabildo and the Plaza San Martin are the main historic sights. Paseo del Buen Pastor is a cultural center in a former convent. The Guemes neighborhood is known for craft markets and evening dining.

Nearby, the Sierras offer day trips to Alta Gracia and to mountain villages.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Córdoba
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Guemes and Nueva Cordoba have many casual places for students and visitors, while the center has traditional places. Look at photos for local sandwiches and grills, and check the opening times, since many places open late.
The summer is hot, and the spring and autumn are comfortable. Many shops close in the afternoon, and restaurants open for dinner after 8 pm. Tip about 10 percent.

faqs.q: What is Córdoba famous for in food?
faqs.a: It is known for the lomito sandwich, empanadas, locro, alfajores and fernet with cola.

faqs.q: Where should I eat in Córdoba?
faqs.a: Nueva Córdoba, Güemes and the center are popular areas. Compare listings on Restroze.

faqs.q: Is Córdoba good for a short trip?
faqs.a: Yes. The old center is walkable and the hills are close.

faqs.q: When do restaurants open in Córdoba?
faqs.a: Dinner usually starts after 8 pm.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in Córdoba?
faqs.a: The Jesuit Block, the Cathedral, Guemes and day trips to the sierras are popular.

argentina/mendoza-province.intro:
Mendoza Province is the heart of Argentine wine, set at the foot of the Andes. Vineyards, olive groves and snow capped peaks make it one of the most scenic food regions in the country.

This page explains what Mendoza Province is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Mendoza Province is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for Malbec and other wines grown at high altitude, in dry sunny conditions, with water from mountain snow melt. Wineries welcome visitors for tours, tastings and lunches, and many have restaurants set among the vines.

The Andes also bring adventure travel, with hiking, rafting, skiing and views of Aconcagua, the highest mountain in the Americas.

Meals here pair beef, lamb and goat with local wines. Asado is the classic, and winery lunches often offer several courses matched with wine. Olive oil, nuts, dried fruit and fresh vegetables from the region appear in local dishes.

Empanadas mendocinas have their own style, with beef, onion and sometimes olives and egg. Alfajores and fruit preserves are common sweets.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Mendoza Province
sections.body:
The wine regions of Maipu and Lujan de Cuyo are close to the city, and the Uco Valley is known for high altitude vineyards and spectacular scenery. Many visitors rent bicycles in Maipu to go between wineries.

The Alta Montana road leads to Uspallata, Puente del Inca and views of Aconcagua. Potrerillos has a lake and rafting.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Mendoza Province
sections.body:
Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. For winery lunches, book ahead and confirm tasting menus and prices, since many require reservations. In the city, the pedestrian streets and tree lined avenues have many restaurants and cafes.

Check the photos for outdoor seating and mountain views.
The harvest in March and April is a lively season, and summer is hot and dry. If you plan to taste wine, arrange a driver or tour, since distances between wineries can be large. Tip about 10 percent.

faqs.q: What is Mendoza Province famous for?
faqs.a: It is famous for Malbec wine, the Andes and winery lunches.

faqs.q: Do I need to book a winery lunch?
faqs.a: Yes, most need a reservation, so book ahead.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Mendoza?
faqs.a: Try asado, empanadas mendocinas, lamb, olive oil products and local wine.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: March and April for harvest, and spring for mild weather.

faqs.q: Is cycling between wineries possible?
faqs.a: Yes in Maipu, where many bike rentals are available.

argentina/mendoza-province/mendoza.intro:
Mendoza is a green and relaxed city set in desert land, with wide sidewalks, plazas and irrigation channels lined with trees. It is the base for exploring the wine country around it.

This page explains what Mendoza is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for wine tourism, outdoor sports and a pleasant outdoor dining culture. After a strong earthquake in the past, the city was rebuilt with wide streets and large plazas, which gives it a calm, open feel.

Many restaurants have terraces and gardens, and evenings are lively on the main avenues.

Local meals often feature grilled beef and lamb, with Malbec poured freely. Empanadas, provoleta, grilled vegetables and fresh salads are common starters. Chivito, grilled goat, is a regional specialty, and sandwiches such as the lomito are popular for a quick meal.

Desserts feature fruit, dulce de leche and local nuts and dried fruits. Olive oil and fruit preserves are good gifts.

Plaza Independencia is the center of the city, and the Parque General San Martin has a lake, a hill with views and a wine museum nearby. The Aristides Villanueva area is known for its evening restaurants.

Day trips to Maipu, Lujan de Cuyo and the Uco Valley are easy, and mountain excursions go toward Uspallata and Aconcagua.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Mendoza
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. For wine focused dinners, look for restaurants with local wine lists and tasting menus. For a casual meal, the avenues have many terraces. Book ahead for evenings in high season.
Summer is hot, so plan outdoor visits in the morning and evening. Winter is cool, with snow in the mountains. A rideshare or tour is safer than driving after wine tasting.

faqs.q: What is Mendoza famous for in food?
faqs.a: Mendoza is famous for Malbec wine, asado, empanadas and winery lunches.

faqs.q: Where should I eat in Mendoza?
faqs.a: The avenues around Aristides Villanueva and the plazas have many options. Compare listings on Restroze.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Mendoza?
faqs.a: Two or three days is enough for the city and a few wineries.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Mendoza?
faqs.a: March to May and September to November are pleasant.

faqs.q: Can I visit wineries without a car?
faqs.a: Yes, by bike in Maipu or by tour.

argentina/misiones.intro:
Misiones is a narrow province in the northeast of Argentina, covered in subtropical forest and famous for the waterfalls at Iguazú. Its food and culture mix Guarani, Jesuit and European settler traditions.

This page explains what Misiones is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The province is known for its red soil, lush jungle, yerba mate fields and Iguazú Falls, one of the greatest waterfall systems in the world. The ruins of Jesuit missions, such as San Ignacio, show the history of the region.

The weather is warm and humid, and the rainforest is home to toucans, coatis and many butterflies.

Local food draws on river fish such as surubi and dorado, cassava, corn and mate. Chipa, a cheesy bread made with cassava starch, is a local favorite, and sopa paraguaya, a dense corn cake, is common. Grilled meats are also eaten here.

Yerba mate is grown across the province, and tereré, the cold version, is common in the heat.

Iguazú Falls and the surrounding national park are the main attraction, with walkways above the water and the dramatic Devil's Throat. San Ignacio Mini is a well preserved Jesuit mission, and Posadas is a river city on the Paraguay border.

The Saltos del Moconá, a long waterfall running parallel to the river, is a remote adventure.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Misiones
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Around the falls, restaurants cater to visitors and offer regional dishes, so check photos and prices. In Posadas, look for places that serve river fish and chipa.
Bring light clothing, insect repellent and a rain jacket. Spring and autumn are comfortable, while summer is hot and humid. Book ahead for holidays.

faqs.q: What is Misiones known for?
faqs.a: It is known for Iguazú Falls, red earth, rainforest and Jesuit missions.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Misiones?
faqs.a: Try river fish, chipa, sopa paraguaya and grilled meats.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: Iguazú Falls, San Ignacio Mini and Posadas are popular.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Spring and autumn are comfortable. Summer is hot.

faqs.q: Is Misiones good for nature lovers?
faqs.a: Yes, for its rainforest and wildlife.

argentina/misiones/puerto-iguazu.intro:
Puerto Iguazú is a small town at the meeting point of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, and the main base for visiting Iguazú Falls on the Argentine side.

This page explains what Puerto Iguazú is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Puerto Iguazú is known for
sections.body:
The town is known as the gateway to the falls, which are a short bus ride away. It sits above the meeting of the Iguazu and Parana rivers, where three countries come together, and a lookout marks the spot at sunset.

The town itself is small and relaxed, with markets, craft shops and restaurants along its main avenue.

Try river fish such as surubi and dorado, grilled or in stews, along with chipa, mandioca, and local sweets. Beef grills are also common, and some places add jungle flavors such as local fruit and honey.

Cafes serve strong coffee and tereré, and pizza and empanadas fill in for a quick meal.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Puerto Iguazú
sections.body:
The Argentine side of Iguazú Falls offers several walkways, including the upper and lower circuits and the Devil's Throat walkway. A boat trip puts you close to the spray. Allow a full day.

The Hito Tres Fronteras, the Guira Oga animal rescue center and the crossing to the Brazilian side can fill another day.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Puerto Iguazú
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Restaurants close to the main street are walkable from most hotels. For dinner after a day at the falls, choose a place close to your hotel, and check hours, since some close early.
Start early at the park to avoid crowds and heat. Bring water, sun protection and a light rain jacket. If you plan to cross to Brazil, check passport rules in advance.

faqs.q: What is Puerto Iguazú known for?
faqs.a: It is known as the gateway to Iguazú Falls and the meeting point of three countries.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Puerto Iguazú?
faqs.a: Try river fish, chipa, grilled meats and local sweets.

faqs.q: How many days do I need?
faqs.a: Two days lets you see the falls and the town without rushing.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to eat?
faqs.a: Browse the main avenue and compare ratings on Restroze.

faqs.q: When should I visit?
faqs.a: Spring and autumn are comfortable and less crowded.

argentina/rio-negro.intro:
Río Negro covers part of northern Patagonia, with the Andes, large lakes, orchards and the Atlantic coast. Its mountain towns are popular for skiing in winter and hiking in summer.

This page explains what Río Negro is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Río Negro is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for the Lake District around Bariloche, with glacial lakes and forested peaks, and for its fruit growing valleys, which produce apples and pears. The coast has beaches and marine wildlife.

The mountain region has a Swiss and German flavor in its food and architecture, from chocolate shops to wooden lodges.

Local cooking includes lamb, trout, venison, wild boar and mushrooms, along with smoked meats and cheeses. Craft beer is a specialty of the Lake District, and fruit from the valleys appears in jams, ciders and desserts.

Chocolate is the regional treasure, with shops selling bars, truffles and hot chocolate with churros.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Río Negro
sections.body:
Bariloche is the center for lakes, ski slopes and hiking. The Circuito Chico loop and the Llao Llao area show lake and mountain views, and Cerro Catedral is the main ski resort.

Nahuel Huapi National Park offers trails and boat trips, and the Atlantic coast has the Bahia de San Antonio and the Las Grutas beach town.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Río Negro
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. In the mountain towns, look for restaurants with lake views and regional dishes such as trout and lamb. In winter, book ahead during school holidays in July.
Winter brings snow and the busiest period. Summer is also popular for hiking. Weather can change fast in the mountains, so carry layers.

faqs.q: What is Río Negro known for?
faqs.a: It is known for the Bariloche lakes, mountains, skiing, fruit valleys and chocolate.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Río Negro?
faqs.a: Try lamb, trout, venison, smoked cheeses, craft beer and chocolate.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: Bariloche, Nahuel Huapi National Park and Cerro Catedral are popular.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: July for skiing and January and February for summer hiking.

faqs.q: Is it good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, with lakes, snow and easy trails.

argentina/rio-negro/bariloche.intro:
Bariloche sits on the shore of Lake Nahuel Huapi, surrounded by the Andes. It is the most visited mountain town in Argentina, loved for hiking, skiing and cozy food.

This page explains what Bariloche is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The town is known for its alpine style buildings of stone and wood, its chocolate shops and its position inside Nahuel Huapi National Park. It is a popular school trip destination for Argentine students and a favorite for honeymooners.

The outdoor life is a big draw, with skiing in winter and hiking, kayaking and cycling in summer.

Bariloche is known for chocolate, and the main street is lined with shops selling bars, truffles and hot chocolate. Regional meals feature smoked trout, venison, lamb, wild boar and mushrooms, often served with local craft beer.

Fondue, hearty stews and berries from the region add to the mountain flavor. Many cafes offer cakes with views of the lake.

The Circuito Chico is a scenic loop of about 60 km with lake views, viewpoints and short walks. Cerro Campanario and Cerro Otto offer views, while Cerro Catedral has ski slopes in winter and walks in summer.

Boat trips lead to Isla Victoria and the Arrayanes forest, and day trips go to El Bolson for its craft market.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Bariloche
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Along the main street, many places cater to visitors. For a quieter meal, look at the lakeside areas and the Llao Llao zone. Check the photos for views and for regional dishes, and book ahead in July and in the peak summer weeks.
Dress in layers, since the weather shifts quickly. In winter, roads may be icy, and shops and restaurants may close early in the low season. Reserve tables for school holidays.

faqs.q: What is Bariloche famous for in food?
faqs.a: It is famous for chocolate, smoked trout, venison, lamb and craft beer.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Bariloche?
faqs.a: July to August for skiing, and December to February for summer hiking.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in Bariloche?
faqs.a: The Circuito Chico, Cerro Campanario, Cerro Catedral and Nahuel Huapi National Park are popular.

faqs.q: Do I need to book a restaurant in Bariloche?
faqs.a: Yes in high season.

faqs.q: Is Bariloche good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, for the lake, snow and many easy activities.

argentina/salta-province.intro:
Salta Province sits in the northwest of Argentina, with red canyons, high deserts, colonial towns and vineyards at some of the highest altitudes in the world.

This page explains what Salta Province is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Salta Province is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for its colorful landscapes, such as the Quebrada de las Conchas and the Calchaqui Valleys, and for its strong Andean culture, expressed in folk music, crafts and food. Cafayate is the center of Torrontes wine.

The pace is slow, and many small towns have a central plaza, a church and an artisan market.

The food of the north is rich in corn, potatoes, quinoa, llama and goat. Empanadas salteñas are famous, usually baked and filled with beef, potato and spices, and eaten with the hands. Locro, humita and tamales are common, along with goat stews.

Torrontes, a fragrant white wine, and high altitude Malbec are the local wines. Sweets include fruit preserves and cheese.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Salta Province
sections.body:
Salta city is the base, with a colonial center and a cable car to a hill with views. The Quebrada de las Conchas road leads to Cafayate, with its wineries and rock formations. Cachi and the Calchaqui Valleys have adobe villages and mountain scenery.

The Train to the Clouds and the Salinas Grandes salt flats are famous excursions. The Humahuaca Gorge is just north in Jujuy.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Salta Province
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. In Salta and Cafayate, look for peñas, restaurants with live folk music in the evening, and for places that serve regional dishes. For a winery lunch, book ahead.
Altitude can cause tiredness, so go slowly on your first day. Distances are long, so plan driving carefully. The dry season from April to October is pleasant, while summer brings rain.

faqs.q: What is Salta famous for in food?
faqs.a: It is famous for empanadas salteñas, locro, humita, goat stews and Torrontes wine.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in Salta Province?
faqs.a: Salta city, Cafayate, Cachi and the Quebrada de las Conchas are popular.

faqs.q: What is a peña?
faqs.a: A peña is a restaurant or venue with live folk music and regional food.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: April to October is dry and comfortable.

faqs.q: Does altitude matter?
faqs.a: Yes, take it easy at first and drink water.

argentina/salta-province/salta.intro:
Salta, nicknamed La Linda, the beautiful, is a colonial city in the northwest, set in a green valley beside the Andes. It is the base for exploring the colorful landscapes of the province.

This page explains what Salta is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for its well kept colonial buildings, its pink cathedral and its folk music tradition. Evenings are lively around the main plaza, with live music in peñas and open air cafes.

Salta also serves as the starting point for the Train to the Clouds and for road trips to Cafayate and the Calchaqui Valleys.

The empanada salteña is the main attraction, small and juicy, with beef, potato, onion and spices. Locro, humita and tamales are also popular, along with goat and llama in some places. Regional sweets use cane syrup, quince and goat cheese.

Regional wines such as Torrontes and high altitude Malbec appear on most menus.

Plaza 9 de Julio, the Cathedral, the Convent of San Bernardo and the MAAM museum of high mountain archaeology are the main sights. The San Bernardo hill has a cable car with views over the valley, and the Mercado Central is lively for local food.

Day trips include the Quebrada de Humahuaca and the road to Cafayate.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Salta
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Peñas near the plaza combine dinner and music, and many open late. For the best empanadas, check the photos and reviews, and look for places with a steady local crowd.
Dinner is late, and peñas can run past midnight. Carry a light jacket for cool evenings. Book ahead for holidays and weekends.

faqs.q: What is Salta famous for in food?
faqs.a: It is famous for empanadas salteñas, locro, humita and regional wines.

faqs.q: What is a peña in Salta?
faqs.a: A peña is a venue with live folk music and regional food.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit in Salta?
faqs.a: The plaza, the cathedral, the cable car and day trips to Cafayate are popular.

faqs.q: When should I visit Salta?
faqs.a: April to October is dry and pleasant.

faqs.q: How do I find a good restaurant in Salta?
faqs.a: Compare ratings and photos on Restroze, and check hours and addresses.

argentina/santa-cruz.intro:
Santa Cruz is a huge province in southern Patagonia, with open steppe, the Andes, huge lakes and the Southern Patagonian Ice Field. Distances are long and the landscapes are dramatic.

This page explains what Santa Cruz is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Santa Cruz is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for Perito Moreno glacier and for the Fitz Roy mountains near El Chalten. The Los Glaciares National Park protects a vast area of ice, lakes and peaks, and is a World Heritage site.

The steppe is home to sheep farms, called estancias, and some welcome guests for lamb barbecues and horse riding.

Patagonian lamb is the highlight, cooked slowly over open fire in a style called cordero al palo. Other local foods include trout, king crab in some parts, and wild game such as guanaco in a few places. Craft beer and chocolate have become popular in the mountain towns.

For dessert, try calafate berry jam and ice cream, since local legend says whoever eats the berry will return to Patagonia.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Santa Cruz
sections.body:
El Calafate is the base for Perito Moreno glacier, with its walkways and boat trips. El Chalten is the trekking capital with trails to Laguna de los Tres and Laguna Torre. The Estancia visits offer a look at rural life.

The coast has Puerto Deseado and the Ruta 40 road, a long classic route.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Santa Cruz
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. In small towns, restaurants may be few, so check hours and book ahead in the high season from December to February. Look for lamb and for places with a warm indoor setting.
Weather can be cold and windy even in summer, so dress in layers. Services are limited outside the main towns, so plan fuel and meals on long drives. Many places close in winter.

faqs.q: What is Santa Cruz known for?
faqs.a: It is known for Perito Moreno glacier, El Chaltén's trekking and Patagonian lamb.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Santa Cruz?
faqs.a: Try cordero al palo, trout, craft beer and calafate berry desserts.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: El Calafate, Perito Moreno glacier and El Chaltén are popular.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: November to March is the main season.

faqs.q: Are distances long?
faqs.a: Yes, plan driving times carefully.

argentina/santa-cruz/el-calafate.intro:
El Calafate is a small town on the shore of Lago Argentino, and the main base for visiting the glaciers of Patagonia. Its restaurants focus on lamb, hearty dishes and warm interiors.

This page explains what El Calafate is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What El Calafate is known for
sections.body:
The town is known as the gateway to Los Glaciares National Park and the Perito Moreno glacier, one of the few glaciers in the world that is stable. Visitors walk along platforms facing the ice and listen to it crack and fall into the lake.

The town itself has a long main avenue with shops, chocolate stores and restaurants.

Patagonian lamb cooked over open fire is the signature dish, often served at restaurants and estancias. You will also find trout, grilled meats, stews and empanadas. Craft beer and calafate berry products are popular.

Chocolate, alfajores and hot drinks are welcome after a cold day outside.

sections.h2: Places to visit in El Calafate
sections.body:
Perito Moreno glacier is the highlight, with walkways and boat trips, and for the adventurous, a guided ice walk. Other glaciers such as Upsala and Spegazzini can be seen on boat tours.

The Glaciarium museum, Laguna Nimez bird sanctuary and estancia day trips are good alternatives. El Chalten is a few hours by road.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in El Calafate
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. The main avenue has many restaurants, so compare menus, hours and photos. In high season, book ahead for dinner and arrange early meals if you have a morning excursion.
Winter is quiet and many places close, so check hours. Summer days are long, so you can plan outings late. The wind is strong, so bring a windproof jacket.

faqs.q: What is El Calafate famous for?
faqs.a: It is famous for its access to the Perito Moreno glacier.

faqs.q: What should I eat in El Calafate?
faqs.a: Try Patagonian lamb, trout, craft beer and calafate berry desserts.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit El Calafate?
faqs.a: November to March is the main season.

faqs.q: Do I need to book dinner in El Calafate?
faqs.a: Yes in high season.

faqs.q: How many days do I need?
faqs.a: Two or three days cover the glacier and the town.

argentina/santa-cruz/el-chalten.intro:
El Chaltén is a small mountain village in the north of Los Glaciares National Park, known as the trekking capital of Argentina. Its cafes and restaurants are built around hungry hikers.

This page explains what El Chaltén is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What El Chaltén is known for
sections.body:
The village is known for Mount Fitz Roy, whose granite peaks rise above the valley, and for a network of trails that start right from the town. It was founded in the 1980s and still feels small and informal.

Most visitors stay a few days to hike, and the evenings are for warm meals and craft beer.

Local meals are hearty, with lamb, stews, pasta, trout and pizzas baked in wood ovens. Craft beer is a local specialty, and cafes serve cakes, hot chocolate and sandwiches for packed lunches.

Vegetarian options are available in many places, since the visitor crowd is varied.

sections.h2: Places to visit in El Chaltén
sections.body:
The trail to Laguna de los Tres leads to the foot of Fitz Roy, and the trail to Laguna Torre leads to a glacier lake with views of Cerro Torre. Shorter walks include the Chorrillo del Salto waterfall and viewpoints close to town.

El Calafate is about three hours away by road.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in El Chaltén
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. The village is small, so most places are within walking distance. Check the hours, since many close after the season, and book dinner for peak months. Pick up packed lunches in the morning from bakeries and cafes.
The weather is changeable and can be cold and windy, so bring layers. Cash is useful in small places. Many businesses close in winter.

faqs.q: What is El Chaltén known for?
faqs.a: It is known for hiking, Mount Fitz Roy and craft beer.

faqs.q: What should I eat in El Chaltén?
faqs.a: Try lamb, stews, pizza, trout and local craft beer.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: November to March is the main season.

faqs.q: Is there vegetarian food?
faqs.a: Yes, many places offer vegetarian dishes.

faqs.q: Do restaurants close in winter?
faqs.a: Many do, so check the hours.

argentina/tierra-del-fuego.intro:
Tierra del Fuego is an island region at the southern end of South America, with mountains, forests, glaciers and cold seas. It is a place of long distances and wild scenery.

This page explains what Tierra del Fuego is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Tierra del Fuego is known for
sections.body:
The island is known as the end of the world, with its southern city of Ushuaia and the Beagle Channel. The Tierra del Fuego National Park protects forests and lakes, and the region is a starting point for cruises to Antarctica.

The cold climate shapes daily life, and warm meals are central to evenings.

The region is known for king crab, called centolla, and for lamb, mussels, hake and other cold water fish. Hearty soups and stews, and grilled meat, are common. Hot chocolate and cakes are welcome treats in the cold.

Craft beer from the south, and regional chocolates, are popular gifts.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Tierra del Fuego
sections.body:
Ushuaia is the main base, with boat trips on the Beagle Channel, trails in the national park and the end of the world train. Lapataia Bay marks the end of Route 3, the road that runs the length of the country.

Rio Grande and Tolhuin are on the Argentine side, and Chile has Puerto Williams across the channel.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Tierra del Fuego
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. In Ushuaia, restaurants focus on seafood, so check the photos for centolla and fish. Book ahead in high season, and confirm hours, as many places close in the low season.
Summer, from December to February, has long days and mild weather, while winter is cold and snowy. Dress in layers and book excursions early.

faqs.q: What is Tierra del Fuego known for?
faqs.a: It is known as the end of the world, with Ushuaia, the Beagle Channel and king crab.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Tierra del Fuego?
faqs.a: Try centolla king crab, lamb, mussels and hake.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: December to February has mild weather and long days.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: Ushuaia, the Beagle Channel and the national park are popular.

faqs.q: Do I need to book ahead?
faqs.a: Yes in high season.

argentina/tierra-del-fuego/ushuaia.intro:
Ushuaia is a port city on the Beagle Channel, with mountains behind it and the sea in front. It is the gateway to Antarctica and one of the most photographed cities in Argentina.

This page explains what Ushuaia is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city calls itself the end of the world, and its position between the Martial mountains and the Beagle Channel is striking. Cruise ships to Antarctica leave from its port, and visitors come for hiking, sailing and wildlife.

The old prison building, now a museum, tells part of the city's history.

The star of the table is the centolla, king crab, served in many ways, from simple boiled crab to gratins and soups. Lamb, fresh fish and mussels are also common. Many restaurants overlook the water and have warm wooden interiors.

For dessert, try chocolate and calafate berry sweets, and enjoy a hot drink after a cold day outside.

The Tierra del Fuego National Park is a short drive away, with trails, forests and Lapataia Bay. Boat trips on the Beagle Channel pass sea lions, cormorants and the lighthouse. The End of the World Train gives a historic ride into the park.

The Martial Glacier has a walk with views over the city. The Maritime Museum and the former prison are worth a visit.

sections.h2: How to choose a restaurant in Ushuaia
sections.body: Use Restroze to compare ratings along with review counts, and open the photos to see the food and setting. Check the address on the map and use the phone number to confirm opening hours before you go. Look for restaurants along the main avenue and the waterfront, and compare menus for centolla. Crab can be expensive, so check prices and portions. Book ahead during the high season.
Weather changes quickly, so carry waterproof layers. Book boat trips early in summer. Some places close in winter, so check the hours.

faqs.q: What is Ushuaia famous for?
faqs.a: It is famous for being the southernmost city, with the Beagle Channel and Antarctic cruises.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Ushuaia?
faqs.a: Try centolla king crab, lamb, mussels and fresh fish.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Ushuaia?
faqs.a: December to February is the main season.

faqs.q: What are the best places to visit?
faqs.a: The national park, the Beagle Channel and the Martial Glacier are popular.

faqs.q: Is Ushuaia expensive?
faqs.a: Prices can be high, especially for crab, so check menus on Restroze.
